title: Spanish flu and an Italian centenarian's memories of wartime
summary: He compares the pandemic to the Spanish flu and recounts a very old Italian teacher saying people never felt today's anxiety during the wars; Shearing's wartime England is similar.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years

blocks.x: Do you have any personal thought about why this has occurred now?

I think that we were lucky that a hundred years went by and didn’t have such a big pandemic going on. Because I think the last event that this, even that can be considered similar to this was the Spanish flu, even though back then I think the numbers of people that died was unbelievable. Like more than the fatalities of the two wars I’ve heard. But you know there is something to be said — I saw an interview of an Italian ex-elementary school teacher that she is still alive, I think one hundred and some years old, and she was saying, very smart, very bright still you know, unbelievable. I was very fascinated. She was saying that she went through, as a little child, the Spanish flu and then the wars, they lost everything. The family lost everything in the first war. She lost everything again in the second war. But she said they never felt like we feel today, the sense of anxiety and stress and preoccupation and — never. Life didn’t stopped during the war. They would © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

go dancing normally during the weekends, and then the alarm would go off and they would try to hide in the basements. But then when the alarm would stop they would go up again to the club and keep dancing. You know? And the same thing, I was reading George Shearing’s biography you know, during the war in England. Guys — they were going out and play gigs every night. And then the planes would come, the Germans, and drop a few bombs, and of course some people died. But it didn’t stop them from running their regular life. So this is something that we should think about. Why is that?
